claims.text: Electrochemical dealloying of a precursor noble-metal high-entropy alloy containing noble and less-noble elements can generate three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Less-noble elements are selectively leached under controlled electrochemical conditions.
Selective leaching leaves an interconnected porous noble-metal framework.
The porous framework provides enhanced catalytic sites.
A suitable precursor is a homogenized multimetal alloy containing noble metals and more chemically active, selectively removable elements.
Electrochemical dealloying in an acidic electrolyte at a controlled potential can selectively dissolve the less-noble elements.
An applied potential sufficient to oxidize the less-noble components can preserve the noble-metal matrix.
The porosity and ligament size of the three-dimensional framework result from selective removal.
The nanoporous framework increases the available catalytic surface area.
Selective dissolution drives surface-diffusion-mediated reorganization of the remaining noble-metal atoms.
Reorganization of the remaining noble-metal atoms forms a robust, interconnected porous network.
Differences in chemical stability enable precise atomic control of the resulting structure.
The resulting NM-HEA nanoframeworks will have high porosity and large surface area.
High porosity and large surface area are beneficial for catalytic activity.
Conventional sputtering or casting produces denser structures than electrochemical dealloying.
Magnetron sputtering or arc melting produces dense, unstructured NM-HEA films lacking catalytically beneficial three-dimensional porosity.
A porous structure may fail to develop if the less-noble component is not effectively leached.
A porous structure may fail to develop if the precursor elements are too similar in chemical stability.
Post-dealloying atomic rearrangements can make precise atomic ordering difficult to control.
The relationship between electrolyte concentration, applied potential, temperature, and the resulting nanostructure remains insufficiently established.

contradictions.description: The mechanism states that dealloying leverages stability differences to achieve precise atomic control, whereas the boundary and uncertainty fields state that atomic ordering may be difficult to control and that the degree of atomic-level control remains unresolved.
